## Chapter 1

The summer of the Spanish War began the Indian summer of life for a man past sixty who wanted only to reap in peace what his years had sown. Contentment came from two sources: the solidarity of old friends in power and the rarer thrill of feeling the game won. In London, 1898, the last survivor of the Legation of 1861 thought himself perhaps the only living man who could enjoy the drama entire. He kept alive in his mind every scene since the Stamp Act—two centuries of disputatious ancestors straining to bring England into an American system—and knew his insignificance in the Civil War, every step of which had the same end. Suddenly, without their help, the blessing fell on Hay. After two hundred years of stupid blundering, England learned her lesson just when Hay would otherwise have faced the old anxieties. To Adams, still breathing Palmerston and John Russell, the rise of Germany as “the grizzly terror,” which in twenty years did what Adamses had tried in vain for two hundred—frightened England into America’s arms—was melodrama worthy of Napoleon the Great. He felt only the satisfaction of seeing the family’s diplomatic obsession at last realized to the profit of his oldest ally.

This was history, not schooling, yet it taught something grave: for the first time he felt a possible purpose at work. At Hay’s table he heard every British Minister discuss the Philippines as a balance-of-power problem in the East, and saw the family labor of a century and a half fall into the grand perspective of empire-building, Hay’s work giving it harmony and ease. No American minister in London had ever finished the arcade with such certainty.

He saw a sequence here where elsewhere he had known only chaos. Porto Rico must be taken; he would have escaped the Philippines. Life on the outskirts teaches little, but it teaches that America must police the West Indies for Europe and for herself; one need not shoulder antipodean archipelagoes when one hesitates to carry those at home. The country decided; he acquiesced, content to be the friend who stands and cheers.

That summer the Camerons set up Surrenden Dering in Kent as a country-house to the Embassy. On a hot July 4 a telegram under the shady trees announced the destruction of the Spanish fleet as tidily as news might have come to Elizabeth in 1588. Later the summons sent Hay to the State Department.

Hay had no wish to be Secretary of State. He preferred London; his friends were as cold. No one knew the strain of the office better, or his want of reserve force. The conclave’s verdict was blunt: a mere place-hunter might decline promotion; a minister of state could not. Refuse—and resign. To Adams, office was poison; it killed—body and soul—physically and socially. Not ambition—that healthy stimulant he had never tasted—but the poison of the will: distortion of sight, warping of mind, coarsening of taste, narrowing sympathy to the emotions of a caged rat. Influence lay in the streets for Hay to stoop and pick up; office promised only annoyance, at the cost of life. Hay obeyed the President with the gloomiest smile he had ever worn; Adams, dark for his friend and darker for himself, shouldered his pack and made for home, arriving none too gladly in La Fayette Square.

He had made another false start and lost two years’ schooling. He had nothing to do with Hay’s politics; their union was to save the personal relation. Mrs. Hay saved it by stopping the Secretary each afternoon for a walk with his friend, tea after, and a chat with any caller.

Freed for his own drift, Adams sailed with the Lodges March 22 for Sicily and Rome. Sicily, from Ulysses to Garibaldi, taught catastrophe and violence; Syracuse, more than Rome, preached anarchy without sequence. Yet Ara Cœli drew all threads to a center: Karnak, Ephesus, Delphi, Mycenæ, Constantinople, Syracuse—roads to the Capitol. New York sent most of all: in forty years America strode to empire so fast that 1860 stood on a horizon with the republic of Brutus and Cato; schoolboys read Abraham Lincoln as they read Julius Caesar; the climax approached as though Sulla were a President and McKinley a Consul. Best to be silent on the Capitol. They added Assisi and St. Francis, whose solution of riddles was the most sufficient ever offered, worth decades more study than Gibbon or the Fathers.

The contrast to what he had taught in 1874 bewildered him. Then, weary of Anglo-Saxon law’s wastes, he had sneered in twelfth‑century Latin at shedding life-blood on Sac and Soc. Not he but Maine and Sohm were fathers of that learning. Having turned to law when religion seemed a blind alley and politics chaos, he found law as futile—no thread stronger than coinage or architecture. St. Francis despised them all and solved the puzzle by rejecting it. Adams went back to Paris broken and contrite, ready to admit his life had no meaning and that it no longer mattered. Solitude did what society had not: it drove him to study his ignorance. Hunted by ennui, he began a triangulation of the twelfth century. The calm, lucid vigor, the little moss-grown churches certain of their purpose, charmed him; but summer was short and churches many; he fell back on the quays and photographs, living for weeks in silence.

John La Farge broke the silence in November. Of men who had affected their friends since 1850, La Farge was foremost. Only he held a mind complex enough to set against American uniformity. The American mind liked to walk straight up, assert or deny a fact, and shout its unconventionality in the conventional idiom. La Farge reversed the process. Quiet, indirect, never separating object from setting, faithful to tradition, abhorring dispute, he carried different shades of contradiction without distress. “Adams, you reason too much!” he would say, even over rice and mangoes in Tahiti. To La Farge, eccentricity was nuance; the truer the tone, the truer the eccentricity.

Whistler, in talk, raged brilliantly against England during the Boer War, and said nothing but what his hearers already thought; La Farge kept silence, an artist’s difference of art. In glass, La Farge’s vehemence flamed; he alone of Americans could use glass like a thirteenth‑century artist. Europe’s glass was dead; modern glass pitiable. Even he felt early glass as document more than living emotion, yet Adams knew hardly a window at Chartres that held its own against La Farge’s color. In talk, La Farge’s mind was opaline; in glass, insubordinate, renaissance, crushing rivalry. He resigned himself to Adams as one who meant well, albeit deplorably Bostonian; and Adams asked no better than to learn.

By mid‑January 1900 Adams got La Farge safely to New York and hurried to Washington. Hay’s troubles were as great as foreseen: endurance doubtful; support uncertain; party jealous. The Boer War fretted Adams worse. He had been taught since childhood, even in England, that 1776 had settled colonial liberty; he refused to sit down in 1900 to prove that Washington was not a felon. If ever England took toward Canada what she took toward the Boers, the United States must insist on 1776. The attitude at home was exceedingly un‑American and terribly embarrassing to Hay. Adams, trained to hold his tongue and keep the machine running, would not bother Hay with theory; Hay’s chance lay in patience till luck turned.

With Hay’s politics Adams had nothing to do. Hay belonged to the New York school of men who played the game better than professionals, for aims larger than pay; but professionals set them aside when possible. McKinley’s solution lay outside Adams’s education: he pooled interests into a general trust, taking each at its own valuation, creating efficiency by management. He found manipulators to match himself; Hay was one, yet the weakest in strength and hardest task. Abroad, help to one side hurt another; Hay thought England must come first, but Germany, Russia, and France combined against her, and the Boer War helped them. Worse, the Senate was unmanageable; a malcontent third could dish any treaty. “A treaty of peace,” said Hay, “ought to be ratified with unanimity in twenty‑four hours. They wrangled six weeks and passed it by one vote. I can settle five or six matters honorably and advantageously; the Senate will reject every one. They would reject any treaty with England; probably any with Russia or Germany.” The Secretary’s real duties reduced to three: fight claims on us; press doubtful claims of our citizens on others; and find offices for friends of Senators when there are none. Was the useless labor worth keeping up?

To Adams the show was old comedy. Foreign legations and domestic factions worked the press and the Senate; obstruction was innocent and open. The Constitution had been meant to neutralize energy; the machine of the fathers could not do the work of a society driven by twenty million horse‑power. Bad machinery added friction; work must still be done.

Always unselfish, generous, patient, Hay had liked the world as it came, laughing and accepting; he would have lived it over just so. Yet constant friction wears out the gayest temper. The old friend faded; equality of indifference shrank within the blank walls of politics; irritations multiplied.

Adams’s new schooling tried to bring twelfth and twentieth centuries into one relation, to correlate political, social, scientific values in movement expressible by mathematics. He cared nothing that the world said it could not be done, or that he knew no formula better than a schoolboy’s s = gt²/2. If Kepler and Newton could take liberties with sun and moon, one might venture to multiply half Congress’s attraction into the square of its time, if only one could find a value—however infinitesimal—for its attraction at any given moment. Historians condemned the attempt as immoral; Adams tried it only because it contradicted all he had taught. He had swept his mind clear. Newcomb was too sound to treat the scheme seriously; the greatest American in science he never met. Langley, accessible and kindly, loved doubt with a physicist’s passion, professed to know nothing between flashes of perception, and, like most physicists, believed in physics. He bowed distantly to philosophy’s problems while doubting their respectability, and put into Adams’s hands a book which the schools had met with silence. Adams read and did not understand; asked and did not get answers. Perhaps this was scientific education possible at sixty: to want mass, not details; unity, not multiplicity. Solar heat was too much or too little; kinetic atoms led to motion, not direction. Everything must be made to move together; one must seek new worlds to measure; and so, on May 12, he settled at the very door of the Trocadéro.


## Chapter 2

Until the Exposition of 1900 closed in November, he haunted it, aching to absorb knowledge and helpless to find it. Langley came by and showed it to him. With a master’s ease Langley threw out all that did not reveal a new application of force—art first, industry next—and led his pupil straight to motors. The new Daimler engine, the automobile become a nightmare at a hundred kilometres an hour, the electric tram only ten years older, threatened to rival the locomotive which was almost Adams’s own age.

Then the great hall of dynamos. Langley confessed he knew little of electricity or force of any kind—his sun might spout more or less heat any day for all he knew. To him the dynamo was channel only; to Adams it became a symbol of infinity. As he grew used to the great gallery, the forty‑foot machines took on moral force, as the early Christians felt the Cross. The planet itself seemed less impressive than this huge wheel, revolving within arm’s length, barely murmuring, not waking a baby nestled at its frame. Before the end, one began to pray to it. Among a thousand symbols of ultimate energy, the dynamo was the most expressive.

Yet between the engine‑house outside and the silent current within, he felt an abysmal break of continuity—no more relation than between the Cross and the cathedral. New rays denied their God; Radium seemed parricidal to Science. A historian who wanted only to be as futile as Langley or Kelvin made a Paradise of ignorance, wrapping himself in vibrations and rays new to man, and lost his arithmetic trying to equate discoveries with economies of force. In seven years man had translated himself into a new universe with no common measure to the old; physics ran stark mad in metaphysics.

Historians arrange sequences and assume cause and effect. Adams had published a dozen volumes to test whether severe selection of facts, in rigorously consequent order, could fix a necessary sequence. It satisfied him no more than Harvard did. Where he saw sequence, others saw something else; no one agreed on a unit of measure. He turned at last to the sequence of force. If all must be reduced to a common value, that value could be only the attraction on his own mind. He would risk translating rays into faith; forces convertible, reversible, interchangeable as they were felt.

On this knife‑edge he crawled between two kingdoms that had nothing in common but attraction. The Virgin’s force was still felt at Lourdes and seemed as potent as X‑rays; in America neither Venus nor Virgin ever had value as force—at most as sentiment. Sex was sin; once it had been strength. The classics invoked it as energy: “Quae quondam rerum naturam sola gubernas.”

From the Virgin he passed to her artist: St. Gaudens at Amiens revealed how the modern American could feel the cathedral's dignity but no longer the force that built it, and Adams understood that the energy he sought to measure had become, for his countrymen, only a question of taste.
